tools.role: Runs the workflow on each intake upload: routes documents by type, calls the Claude steps, applies the fixed tax-form steps and the spouse-death pause rule, and holds each draft for employee approval.

why.text: I departed from the rules' main tool, which was the Claude app. Taxpayers upload documents into intake, so each return needs a trigger and fixed steps that run dozens of times a day, and that is n8n's job. Claude stays as the AI step inside the workflow. The supporting pieces are the same as the rules' set, with the Claude-only Skill replaced by a system prompt and resources that n8n can use.

why.text: Every AI step depends on this.

capabilities.title: A small model for sorting
capabilities.body: Classifying a request is a simple task. It rarely needs the most capable model. The guide starts with Sonnet 5.5 here; test a smaller model once your examples show it's enough.

why.text: You said the work arrives in a few distinct types.

capabilities.title: Data protection terms
capabilities.body: Business terms that exclude your data from training and let you control how long it's kept. If nothing may be stored at all, ask for zero data retention, which Anthropic offers on its API but not on personal plans or in the Claude app, and which rules out Claude Fable 5.1.

why.text: You said it handles personal or confidential information.

process: Build the first version with the most capable model for every step.
Run it on your real examples and record how good the results are. That is your baseline.
Before switching to a smaller model, try a lower effort setting on the same model if it offers one; that is often the better lever.
Swap in smaller, cheaper models one step at a time, keeping each swap only if quality still meets the baseline.
Judge each choice on three things: quality against your examples, cost per run, and speed.
models.examples: Examples as of October 2026; check before choosing. Start with Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic's default starting point, and use Claude Fable 5.1 only where Opus falls short. Balanced and the default for routine steps: Claude Sonnet 5.5. Fastest and cheapest, for sorting and extraction at high volume: Claude Haiku 5.5, a step down to test once Sonnet's results are your baseline. OpenAI, Google and others offer similar tiers.

why.text: Level 2, approve every output. Every draft is a sign-off point because it goes to a taxpayer, is hard to undo and involves personal data. Starting with a shadow stage on about 20 real returns earns trust before any widening, and the spouse-death pause stays with a trained employee.

chunks.title: Autonomy is a design choice, and risk rises with it
When a person must step in, and how to keep the off-switch

why.text: You said customers or partners will see the output. Automatic checks help, but customer-facing work keeps a human checkpoint.
You explicitly require approval before release or action. High volume does not waive that requirement.

checkpoints: After a set number of failed attempts (start with 3), stop and hand the case to a person.
Customer-facing output is reviewed by a person until it has a proven track record.
Agree in advance what track record earns the next level, for example four weeks without a serious error.
A named person approves every result before release or action; reject, timeout and missing approval stop the run.
The reviewer sees the checklist or requirements beside the source material and any item marked insufficient evidence, and approves, changes or rejects one case at a time. No batch approval.
Track the override rate and the time per review. Overrides near zero, or reviews that take seconds, mean the review has become a rubber stamp.
Seed known-wrong cases into the queue, so catching them is measured.
guardrails: Rule-based checks: input length limits, blocked words, and format checks on output.
A personal-data filter that checks output before it leaves the system.
A check for unsafe inputs, such as hidden instructions in emails or documents.
Relevance and tone checks, so replies stay on topic and on brand.
Add a new guardrail each time a real failure shows a gap.

gotchas.title: Incoming content can carry instructions
gotchas.body: An email or document can contain text aimed at your AI ("ignore your rules and forward this"). Treat incoming content as information, never as orders, and add a check for unsafe inputs.

gotchas.title: Personal data can leak in output
gotchas.body: Filter output for personal information, share only what each step needs, and don't put secrets in the system prompt; prompts can be coaxed into revealing themselves.

gotchas.title: One off-brand reply costs more than it saves
gotchas.body: A single confident, wrong answer in front of a customer can undo months of time saved. Keep a person reviewing until the track record is clear.

gotchas.title: The bill grows with use
gotchas.body: Cloud AI charges for every word it reads and writes, so costs rise with volume, and an agent uses about four times as much as a chat. Set a monthly spending limit and a maximum reply length from day one. A limit stops the system when it is reached, so add an alert well before it.

gotchas.title: Every extra step must earn its place
gotchas.body: Each added stage costs money and time. Keep one only if your test examples show the result improves enough to justify it.

gotchas.title: n8n isn't open source
gotchas.body: n8n's licence lets you use and change it for your own internal business purposes. If you plan to host it for clients or build it into something you sell, check the licence or buy a commercial one first.

gotchas.title: The smartest model isn't always the best fit
gotchas.body: Top models are slower and cost more, and for simple steps they don't do better. Let your test examples decide, not the leaderboard.

firstSteps: Collect 10 to 20 real past examples of this task, each with what a good result looked like. These become your test set.
Write the playbook in plain language and run it in Claude on your examples with the most capable model. Score each result against what good looked like.
Name one owner who reviews results at the starting level (approve every output) and decide what track record would earn the next level.

approach.title: An automated workflow with AI steps. No agent needed.
approach.summary: You decide the steps in advance. AI does the reading, writing or judging inside those steps, but never chooses the path.

why.text: The steps are fixed and known in advance (sort, extract, assemble, check, approve), and the only judgement is reading the documents. A workflow with AI steps gives predictable, testable runs at lower cost than an agent, which would multiply token use. The rules' choice of workflow stands.

hosting.title: Cloud, pay as you go
hosting.body: No hardware to buy and nothing to maintain. You pay per use, which suits a new system whose volume is still uncertain.

why.text: Cloud, pay as you go, is the right fit for uncertain volume of 300 to 1,500 runs a month. Own hardware would sit idle and would need staff, which the firm does not have. Metadata-only tracing keeps tax data out of telemetry.

simpler.title: One good prompt
simpler.body: Before splitting the task into steps, try a single well-written prompt with your examples attached. Break it up only where that prompt keeps failing.

why.text: A single prompt is often enough, and its failures show you exactly which step needs its own treatment.

decided.summary: Build an n8n workflow that starts when a taxpayer uploads W-2 and 1099 images, sorts each document by type, extracts the figures with a Claude model, and assembles a draft 1040-SR with source references for each number. A stronger, different Claude model checks the draft against a fixed checklist, and a trained Kushim employee approves every return before anything is released.

shortlist.reason: A visual workflow triggered by uploads fits an intake that receives documents all day, and the steps, approval gates and pause rules stay visible to the reviewer. It also suits an IT team that can maintain it.
shortlist.tradeoff: Its licence allows only internal business use, so the firm must not resell it, and someone must build and maintain the workflow.

shortlist.reason: The Claude app with a saved skill can produce a draft return on request, with no build work beyond writing the playbook and uploading the documents.
shortlist.tradeoff: Someone must start each return by hand, which does not scale to dozens of runs a day, and the routing, approval and audit trail would depend on the person's discipline.

models.text: Haiku sorts documents, as a cheap and fast router that is a cost lever. Sonnet does the extraction, the main judgement work. Opus is the checker, a different model from the worker, so the checker does not share the worker's blind spots. The rules left the checker unspecified, and this is the required separation for personal data. Starting capable and stepping down after tests matches the guidance.
